name: AI in Education
blurb: Artificial intelligence is already in schools, in the tools teachers plan with, the software students practise on, and the systems that run buses and budgets. These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

children.name: Getting Oriented
children.blurb: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: The Classroom
children.blurb: Part II, The Classroom, covers AI in each stage and subject. It begins with preschool through second grade, then turns to reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring.

children.name: Every Student, Every Family
children.blurb: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Running the School
children.blurb: Part IV, Running the School, covers teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. These chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members.

sections.body: This part of school life is the whole of a school's use of AI, not just its operations, because a school is also responsible for what AI does to how children learn and for protecting children while it happens. The book describes AI in education as a field where the same kind of tool can help or harm depending on how adults design and supervise its use, and it points to two trials that produced opposite results for that reason. It gathers 300 practical ideas across 20 chapters, from preschool through graduation and from the classroom to the business office, each carrying an evidence label. The labels are honest about how young the field is and tell readers how much weight each idea can bear.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, the book finds, is AI tutoring that teachers design and supervise, with teachers writing the opening prompt and staying in the room, and clear personal messages to families about missed work, grades and absences. What does not work is students using plain chatbots on their own, where most copy answers and later score worse, and AI detectors, which misclassify writing by students still learning English so a detection score must never be treated as proof. The book also says no evidence shows online monitoring prevents harm, no independent evaluation of AI security systems in schools was found, and research on young children and students with disabilities is thin. The rule it holds to is that people make every decision that affects a student, student names and details stay out of any tool without a signed data privacy agreement, tools give hints rather than answers, every AI draft is checked by a person, and every flag leads to a person who reaches out. Adoption fails when leaders mandate tools they do not use, reward logins instead of results and skip the rules, and succeeds when leaders model use, measure hours saved and student outcomes, and publish the rules for privacy, review and accountability.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from orientation to the classroom, then to families, then to the running of the school. Getting Oriented gives the reader the frame for the whole Volume, the evidence labels, the five rules and the argument that tools do not change schools and the people in them do, so a teacher, leader or parent starts here to understand how to weigh every later idea. The Classroom is where teachers go for the practical ideas on planning, teaching, feedback and grading, organized by subject and grade, and where the lesson of the two trials is applied to daily instruction. Every Student, Every Family speaks to parents and to staff who work with them, covering how children use AI, how the school protects them, and the questions families should be able to ask, including the five questions in Chapter 14 with the answers a good school gives. Running the School is for principals, district leaders and board members, covering policy, pilots, purchasing and professional learning, and closing each chapter with the question a board should ask, the evidence needed to answer it, the failure pattern that trips districts up, and a Thirty Day Move any school can take, with the final chapter laying out the first 90 days for a superintendent, a principal, a teacher and a parent.
